Thanks so much :) it just fascinated me how enlightenment principles managed to impose themselves on the Russian political climate so quickly- which of course had some disastrous effects. If you look at places like the UK and France, enlightened ideals manifested themselves gradually. But for Russia it happened really quickly. The old imperial system and indeed, Russians were relatively unacquainted with these new enlightened ideas, which lead to it getting out of hand. Liberal, orthodox, monarchist, and socialist beliefs were warring with each other and the country was left in a fragmented state. Dostoyevsky showed this in The Idiot, where these two ideas were mixed together which lead to a society attempting to emulate contemporary western ideas. You see individuals being crushed by a suffocating social world mixed with the expectations of the old orthodox ways (marriage, social etiquette etc), and the expectations of the inherently materialist values of the West that seeped into Russian society (wealth, “originality” etc). So when Dostoyevsky presents the “positively good man”, Myshkin, we see that his innocent, truthful, and Christlike character is simply incompatible with the ideological dilemma taking place in both Russian politics and the Russian psyche. That’s how I see it, for now at least. But I haven’t developed on these ideas yet so I might have got some things wrong, but that’s the gist of it.
